source_refs.note: Exercise 3.4, Question 10: Exercise 3.4, book page 94: Q1-Q15 (integration by partial fractions); answers book pages 301-302

blocks.explanation:
It looks like a long Case-II question (four constants), but first test whether the numerator shares a factor with the denominator.
At \(x = -1\) the numerator is 0, so \(x + 1\) is a factor; in fact the numerator is \((x + 1)^2(x + 2)\).
Plan: factorise the numerator, cancel, and integrate the simple fraction that remains.
steps:
Given: \(\int \frac{x^3 + 4x^2 + 5x + 2}{(x + 1)^3(x + 2)}\,dx\).
To find: the integral.
Method: look for common factors first (factor theorem); cancelling saves the whole partial-fraction work.

Test the numerator at the roots of the denominator
\[x = -1:\ -1 + 4 - 5 + 2 = 0\]
\[x = -2:\ -8 + 16 - 10 + 2 = 0\]
Why: Factor theorem: if \(p(a) = 0\), then \(x - a\) is a factor of \(p(x)\).

Factorise the numerator
\[x^3 + 4x^2 + 5x + 2 = (x + 1)(x^2 + 3x + 2)\]
\[= (x + 1)(x + 1)(x + 2) = (x + 1)^2(x + 2)\]
Why: Divide by \(x + 1\) to get \(x^2 + 3x + 2\), which factorises as \((x + 1)(x + 2)\).

Cancel
\[\dfrac{(x + 1)^2(x + 2)}{(x + 1)^3(x + 2)} = \dfrac{1}{x + 1}\]
Why: For \(x \ne -1, -2\) the common factors cancel.

Check
\[(x + 1)^2(x + 2) = (x^2 + 2x + 1)(x + 2)\]
\[= x^3 + 4x^2 + 5x + 2 \;\checkmark\]
Why: Expanding the factorised form gives back the numerator. (Partial fractions would give the same: \(A = 1\) and all other constants 0.)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In the answers at the end of the book (page 302), the answers of Exercise 3.4 are printed under the wrong heading "Exercise 3.6". The answer of this question is item (x) of that block: \(\ln|x + 1| + c\). That answer is correct. The block headed "Exercise 3.4" (page 301) belongs to a different exercise.
